title: The US is banning foreign robots
summary: The U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced an import ban on advanced robotic devices and power inverters from foreign countries, targeting mobile robots like humanoid and quadruped models. While officially not country-specific, the ban will significantly impact China's robotics industry as it expands humanoid robot production.
content:
The Chinese robot maker, Unitree, will likely be impacted by the ban. | Bloomberg via Getty Images	

The US government is targeting China with a new import ban on "advanced robotic devices" and power inverters made in foreign countries, as reported earlier by Reuters. In an announcement on Tuesday, the Federal Communications Commission says the ban will include "mobile" robots, such as humanoid and quadruped models - but it is not limited to robots that walk around.
Though the FCC says the move isn't targeted at a specific country, it will have a major impact on China as the country ramps up efforts to produce humanoid robots, some of which we've seen in viral videos stumbling to Michael Jackson, partaking in MMA fights, and even appearing …
Read the full story at The Verge.

title: This comfy gaming headset that can play audio from two sources is $25
summary: The EPOS H3 Hybrid gaming headset is on sale for $24.99 (75% off) at Woot, offering an unusual combination of wired (USB-A and 3.5mm) and Bluetooth connectivity that allows simultaneous audio from multiple sources. The headset features a balanced sound profile, comfortable fit, dual microphones, and up to 37 hours of battery life, making it a budget-friendly option for players seeking flexibility.
content:
The Hybrid adds Bluetooth functionality to the wired H3, seen here. | Photo by Cameron Faulkner / The Verge	

While most gaming headsets have moved towards low-latency wireless connections, there’s something to be said for a budget-friendly, capable wired headset. The EPOS H3 Hybrid is on sale for just $24.99 at Woot, a whopping 75 percent off its original price of $99.99. It has an unorthodox batch of features: USB-A and 3.5mm options for connecting to a controller or a PC, and Bluetooth support for listening to music and taking calls. Notably, it can play audio from wired and wireless sources concurrently, and it can last up to 37 hours per charge.
EPOS H3 Hybrid

Where to Buy:

 $99.99 $24.99 at Woot

My colleague Cameron Faulkner spent some time with the wired-only version of this headset five years ago, and was impressed by its balanced sound profile, comfortable fit, and generously-sized volume knob. He had some qualms about USB connectivity and lack of sidetone, both of which seem to have been addressed in the Hybrid version of the headset that’s available at a steep discount right now. This version also has two microphones — a removable boom mic and a built-in microphone — so you can still take calls via Bluetooth without looking like an airline pilot.

User-replaceable batteries will be the law in Europe in February 2027, but instead of bringing them to the rest of the world, Logitech plans to ship one version of its wireless mice to Europe and a different version everywhere else.
That's the word from Logitech's new gaming boss, Robin Piispanen. We talked about it over iced vanilla lattes at my local cafe, right after discussing how Logitech isn't sure it wants to make another gaming handheld.

title: Tile’s best Bluetooth tracker is down to its lowest price of the year
summary: The Tile Pro Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $23.99 (lowest price of 2026), offering 500-foot range and 110-decibel alerts for both Android and iOS users, along with features like two days of location history and Place Alerts that Apple's AirTag doesn't provide. Unlike AirTag, the Tile Pro includes a built-in keyring and optional subscription services for emergency response features.
content:
The Tile Pro offers the longest Bluetooth range of any Tile tracker. | Image: Tile	

Apple’s latest AirTag may seem like the obvious choice if you own an iPhone and are shopping for a Bluetooth tracker, but it’s not the most affordable option. For families that contain both Android and Apple devices, it might be better to pick up the latest Tile Pro instead. It works well across both platforms, and right now it’s on sale for $23.99 ($11 off) at Amazon and directly from Tile. This is its cheapest price in 2026 so far and only $1 shy of the all-time low we saw in October.
Tile Pro

Where to Buy:

 $34.99 $23.99 at Amazon
 $34.99 $23.99 at Tile

As Tile’s most capable tracker, the Pro offers a Bluetooth range of up to 500 feet and the loudest ring of its lineup at 110 decibels, making it easier to locate misplaced items nearby. While it doesn’t tap into Apple’s Find My or Google’s Find Hub networks, its Life360 app remains a reliable option for keeping tabs on valuables both near and far. 
The Tile Pro can also save you a little money in a few ways compared to Apple’s AirTag.  For starters, it includes a built-in keyring hole, so you can attach it to your keys, backpack, or luggage without buying a separate holder. On top of that, Tile includes a handful of free extras that Apple doesn’t provide, like two days of location history and Place Alerts that notify you when members of your Life360 Circle arrive at or leave certain places. If you’re willing to pay for a subscription (which starts at $7.99 a month) you’ll also gain access to features like SOS alerts that can connect you to emergency services, crash detection, roadside assistance, and even free towing depending upon the plan you choose.

title: You don’t need to splurge on an expensive handheld fan to beat the heat
summary: Affordable JisuLife handheld fans priced at $25-33 offer a practical alternative to premium options like Dyson's $99-150 models, with comparable battery life and functionality. Budget-conscious consumers can achieve effective personal cooling without premium brand pricing.
content:
It’s not fancy, but it gets the job done for hours and hours on a single charge.	

Despite what influencers may say, you don’t need to spend $99.99 on Dyson’s HushJet Mini Cool or $149.99 for the Shark ChillPill to survive the summer whenever you leave the comfort of air-conditioning. My family has found all the comfort it needs to survive humid baseball games, sweltering concerts, and sweaty hikes with a couple of affordable handheld fans from a Chinese company called JisuLife that has spent the past decade honing its hardware.
At the start of the summer, I impulse-purchased a pair of JisuLife Life10 S fans from Costco, which at CDN $25 each (or $32.99 through Amazon), are among the most basic offerings from the company. JisuLife’s extensive lineup includes some fan models costing close to $100 with features like reverse-charging to power your phone and 100 different speed settings. I want all those features, but my goal was to not spend several hundred dollars on personal cooling devices that could easily go missing or get damaged during the chaos of summer activities.
The Life10 S’ functionality is comparatively basic, but also easy to use. A sliding power switch on the back prevents it from accidentally turning on while banging around inside a backpack, and a single button on the front cycles through five different fan speeds. There’s also a basic LCD display showing the battery’s remaining charge when the fan is first powered on and the current speed setting. It’s simple, but the Life10 S does its one job quietly and for a surprisingly long time.
When Dyson announced its first handheld fan in April, I assumed the company that had developed an expertise in moving air had created a personal cooling device that would outperform everything else on the market. My spouse loves their Dyson hair dryer, and I was sure the HushJet Mini Cool would be my secret weapon for surviving hot and humid summers, even if at $99 it was a splurge. But having used both Dyson’s persona
